title: Slow Cortical Potential Neurofeedback
subtitle: Training very slow shifts in cortical excitability
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating slow cortical potential neurofeedback within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain slow cortical potential neurofeedback without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in slow cortical potential neurofeedback.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to slow cortical potential neurofeedback.

sections.explainSimply: SCP training teaches regulation of slow voltage shifts associated with changing cortical activation thresholds.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: The learner is cued to produce more negative or positive shifts, with transfer trials sometimes removing feedback.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: SCP protocols have been studied particularly in ADHD and epilepsy contexts. Acquisition demands DC-capable equipment and rigorous artifact control.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Choosing a camera lens: every method emphasises some information and introduces its own distortions.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand slow cortical potential neurofeedback to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Eye movement and drift can contaminate very slow potentials.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using slow cortical potential neurofeedback predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Eye movement and drift can contaminate very slow potentials. Evidence classification: promising in selected research protocols; mixed clinical evidence.
